title: Taken with a kiss (Deuteronomy Rabbah 11:10)
hookLine: God takes Moses' soul with a kiss
tomorrow: the sea won't split until someone steps in. who goes first?

lines: LAST DAYS HAVE THEIR OWN PACE.
cards: Last days have their own pace. The last shift before a job ends, the last practice of a season, the last night in a house before the movers come. People walk slower.
They touch door frames. They take one more look out a window they know by heart. This is a lesson about an ending, and it's a tender one: how the rabbis imagined Moses' last moment.

teach.b: The Torah tells Moses' death in one plain line: "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD." In Hebrew, according to the word is al pi, literally, by the mouth.
The rabbis heard that and asked: what does it mean to die by the mouth of God? Their answer: a kiss. Deuteronomy Rabbah tells it slowly, the way you would tell it to a child at bedtime.
When the time comes, Moses' soul doesn't want to leave the body it has lived in. God doesn't send a messenger to drag it out. God comes close, and takes Moses' soul with a kiss.
One to tell a friend tonight: the rabbis built a whole tender scene out of a single Hebrew phrase, by the mouth. And notice what it doesn't do.
It doesn't say Moses was eager to go; his soul hesitates.
It doesn't pretend an ending isn't one.
It says the ending was near, personal and kind, from the one the Torah says knew Moses face to face. The Talmud names others who died this way, Aaron and Miriam among them.
Jewish life is honest about grief, with days of sitting, a prayer for mourners, neighbors at the door. And beside all that, this one picture: an ending that came as a kiss.

how: Jewish mourning practices include sitting shiva with the family, saying the Mourner's Kaddish, and visitors bringing food; the rabbinic phrase 'death by a kiss' is used for a gentle passing.

games.q: what does “taken with a kiss” mean?
o: a gentle death: the soul taken by God's kiss

his soul hesitates; the midrash doesn't pretend an ending is easy.

al pi. the rabbis read it as a kiss.

games.q: your coach is retiring, and Saturday is the last game. the team wants to mark it. what fits the midrash's picture of an ending?
o: something close and personal: thank-yous said face to face.
skip it; a fuss only makes endings harder for everyone.
a huge show, loud enough that nobody has to feel sad.
games.why: in the midrash, God comes near and ends Moses' life with a kiss: an ending that is close, personal and kind, without pretending it isn't one.

practice: Bring to mind one ending in your life right now, small or large: a season, a job, a friendship shifting, a home. Count three things it gave you, slowly, one on each breath.
Then thank it, quietly, the way you'd thank someone at the door on their way out.

wordCard.voice: Taken with a kiss: the rabbis' reading of Moses' death by the mouth of God. Close, personal and kind.

orig.note: Hebrew: by the mouth (of). Deuteronomy 34:5's 'according to the word of the LORD', read by the rabbis as a kiss.

carryVoice: Taken with a kiss: an ending can come close, and kind, and still be an ending. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD.
